CoverSure/Policy Portfolio /Product design

Banners were the obvious answer. I shipped conditions instead.

Five capabilities had to become discoverable on the screen where people manage their policies. Rather than give each one a promotional slot, I gave each one a condition — a rule about when it becomes useful to this particular user, checked against their actual portfolio.

5→7 capabilities became conditions
0 new features built
11 real screens shipped
Product Designer· UX strategy · recommendation logic · information hierarchy · progressive disclosure · UX writing Shipped

Shipped recently, so there is no usage data yet. Rather than borrow a number I can't stand behind, I wrote the plan that would prove me wrong — every claim below as a hypothesis, with the threshold that falsifies it. Read the measurement plan →

Six decisions · ~3 min scan · Open Know more for the reasoning behind any one

01UX Strategy

I changed the question, not the layout.

Not how do we promote these five features? but when does each one become useful to this user? The first question only has placements you can argue about. The second has an answer you can build — and check against data the product already holds.

Rejected IF a capability needs adoption → THEN put a banner on the busiest screen

02Systems thinking
Recommendation logic

Every capability had to earn its place.

Seven capabilities, seven conditions, one rule set. The screen composes itself from whichever conditions are true for that person — and never offers more than two actions at a time.

Nothing addedNo policies, no report

Policies addedRatings, then suggestions

Identical layout, identical feature set. Only which conditions are true changes — and the buy suggestions sit below the policies in every single state.

The strongest decision was the one I didn’t ship.

Advisor Portfolio — a monetisable feature under adoption pressure — got no entry point on this screen at all. The Homepage already provides one. Repeating it here would have added noise without adding access.

Declined Advisor needs adoption → add an Advisor banner to Portfolio

HomepageThe advisor route that already exists

The Homepage already carries the CoverRisk score, the coverage meter and the advisor route. The access was never missing — only the banner was.

CoverSure · Policy Portfolio Scan version

UX Strategy

I changed the question, not the layout.

The tension

Business needed five capabilities adopted. Users came to Portfolio to check a premium date, find a policy number, or see what had lapsed. Both needs were real, and they pointed in opposite directions.

What I decided

No capability gets a permanent promotional slot. Each one gets a condition — a statement about when it becomes useful — evaluated against the user’s actual portfolio.

Why, and what I rejected

A banner does not fail because it is badly placed. It fails because it interrupts someone mid-task with an offer they have no way to evaluate — and some of them stop opening the section at all. That is the part that made the default answer expensive rather than merely ineffective.

How do we promote this? has no answer you can build. It only has placements you can argue about in a review. When does this become useful? resolves to a rule — and a rule can be checked against data the product already holds.

Which reframes the conflict rather than splitting it. Business needs adoption. Users need relevance. A condition serves both, because a capability shown at the moment it is useful is both more discoverable and less annoying than one shown permanently.

How it shows up on screen

The layout never changes between users. What changes is which conditions are true — which is why the same screen can look sparse for one person and dense for another without either being a different design.

Systems thinking · Recommendation logic

Every capability had to earn its place.

The tension

Seven capabilities, one screen, and a finite amount of attention. A rule set that fires everything at once is just a banner stack with extra steps.

What I decided

Four stages, running as a loop rather than a funnel:

Understand — what do we know? Policies held, family members added, CoverRisk report status, each policy’s KYP rating, onboarding answers.
Prioritise — what matters most here? Not every gap is equally urgent, and not every product is equally foundational.
Guide — show one or two useful next actions. Never ten. The ceiling is the design.
Adapt — the user acts, context changes, Portfolio changes.

Why, and what I rejected

Adapt is not a fourth stage at the end — it is the edge that closes the loop. The user acting is what produces new information, and that information returns through Understand. This is the whole difference between a system and a smarter banner: the next recommendation is better than the last one because of what the user just did.

Add a policy and the measured gap shrinks. Finish CoverRisk and categories turn into amounts. Add family and the prompt stops appearing, because its condition is no longer true.

The two-action ceiling was the constraint I defended hardest. Every capability owner wants their entry point visible, and each individual request is reasonable. The ceiling is what stops seven reasonable requests from adding up to an unusable screen.

How it shows up on screen

Four more real states. None is a layout variant — each is a different condition being true, and the screen composes itself accordingly.

Group health onlyPremium reads “—”

One policySparse, not empty

Inactive foundLapse surfaced

Full familyPrompts gone

On group-only cover, Premium Yearly reads “—” because the user does not pay it. Showing a number there would have been a lie of convenience.

Product judgment

The strongest decision was the one I didn’t ship.

The tension

Advisor Portfolio is a monetisable feature with adoption pressure behind it, and Portfolio is the busiest screen in the product. Every incentive pointed at putting a banner there.

What I decided

No advisor entry point on Portfolio. Instead, the advisor is offered immediately after CoverRisk generates the user’s report — the moment they have context, and probably questions.

Why, and what I rejected

Users already have a direct route from the Homepage. Repeating it on Portfolio would have added noise without adding access — the access was never the missing part.

There was also a second entry point already competing for the same space. The PRO tier’s relationship manager handles claims, legal questions and whatever else goes wrong; Advisor Portfolio is specifically guidance on cover. Two genuinely different needs — stacking them on one screen would have blurred both.

Placed after a report, the same action reads as useful rather than promotional, because by then the user has something specific to ask about. Declining to place a feature is harder to argue for than placing one — and it is the decision I would defend first.

What I didn’t control

The PRO subscription banner on this screen carries over from the previous design and sits outside this scope. It is already being repositioned in an upcoming update. Worth naming plainly: the conditions described here govern the entry points I owned, not every pixel on the screen.

Decision design · Personalisation

A number they could disagree with.

The tension

CoverRisk already collected age, location, family, dependants, health, lifestyle, income, investments, property and expenses — then produced a recommended coverage amount that stayed inside its own report. Meanwhile the buying screen, where a number would actually change someone’s mind, showed a category name.

What I decided

Connect the existing report back to the buying moment. No new data, no new model — just the number placed where the decision happens: Understand → Recommend → Quantify → Buy.

Why, and what I rejected

Most people do not know what cover they need. Left alone, they optimise the one number they understand — the premium — and buy the cheapest policy available. Then treatment takes away their income and they discover the cover was never built for their life. That is exactly what critical illness cover exists for, and it is invisible to anyone shopping on price.

So the recommendation names a coverage level and the average premium for it at that age and health profile. Not a specific insurer. Not a cheap policy. The rejected version of this was a personalised-looking banner that still optimised for click-through on the cheapest available plan.

The point of showing the inputs is that the user can now disagree with the number — and a recommendation you can argue with is the only kind worth trusting.

The same principle, second proof: KYP

A policy rating on its own is just a badge. So the rating ships as a plain-language verdict with a count of how many conditions work in the user’s favour and how many do not — and it sits on the policy card in the listing, where they are already scanning what they own. On the policy itself, Know Your Policy became a tab beside Details, at the same depth as the policy’s own information.

Rating scaleVerdict + condition counts

A room-rent cap is the clause nobody reads and everybody discovers at the worst possible time. The counts are what make it findable at all.

Product ethics · Prioritisation

We ranked protection, not the catalogue.

The tension

A recommendation system is only as good as its ranking — and ranking is exactly where commercial pressure lands, because some products are simply easier and more profitable to sell.

What I decided

Three tiers, worked through with Product and Design leadership rather than designed in isolation. Foundational (Health, Life) — absence here is the gap a family feels first, and nothing outranks it. Additional (Super Top-Up, Critical Illness, Accident) — these extend cover rather than establish it. Situational (Hospicash, Home) — relevant to some, irrelevant to most, shown only when something in the user’s context asks for it.

Why, and what I rejected

An important separation: CoverRisk does not decide this order. It supplies the coverage amount and the premium estimate. The sequence is a separate decision, and it holds regardless of what the report returns — which is what stops the ranking from drifting toward whatever is easiest to sell that quarter.

Pushing a lower-priority product because it converts better creates the wrong outcome for the user, and that damage lands on the brand rather than on the campaign. Portfolio recommends what matters next, not what is easiest to promote.

This is also the decision most likely to be quietly reversed later under revenue pressure, which is why it is written down as an explicit ordering rather than left to whoever configures the next campaign.

The honest caveat

The bars on the previous screen show relative priority in the recommendation order. They are not measured data, and nothing here should be read as a conversion figure.

Behavioural UX · UX writing

The reason arrives before the ask.

The tension

Share Policy needed adoption, and the obvious move was another button. But a button on the policy screen competes with Edit Details — and loses, because sharing has no obvious payoff at the moment you are looking at it.

What I decided

The question was never where should Share Policy go? It was when does sharing become useful enough to act on? So on Life and Group policies the entry point stopped being a button and became a sentence — and the card sits after the policy details rather than competing with them.

Why, and what I rejected

Sharing an insurance policy is not a convenience. It is a responsibility, and the moment it pays off is the worst moment of someone’s life — a nominee hunting for a policy number while grieving. You cannot design for that moment. You design ahead of it.

Which is why the reason has to lead. An action with no stated stake is just another button; the same action with the nominee named becomes something a person can decide about.

Worth being straight about: the card that shipped makes this argument more loosely — “While any emergency, share policy with family members will be helpful.” Tightening that into a line that names the nominee and the moment is the UX-writing half of this decision, and it is still working its way through.

The same principle, second proof: Family Overview

One person usually manages insurance for a whole family, so a missing member means missed renewals and a harder emergency. The Family Overview answers three questions at a glance: who is covered (every member, their policy count, their yearly premium), who is missing, and whose policies still need adding.

An incomplete overview reads as incomplete. That is the whole thesis applied to an adoption problem — let the structure carry the request instead of a banner asking for it.

The incomplete row is the reminder. A member with nothing added reads as unfinished work rather than as a marketing prompt.
